title: Pentatonic and blues
summary: Minor and major pentatonic scales, the blues scale, five positions, lead techniques, the 12-bar blues, and first improvisation.

lessons.title: The minor pentatonic scale
lessons.summary: Learn the five-note scale behind most rock and blues solos and play it in its first box position.

steps.title: Five notes
steps.body:
A **pentatonic scale** has five notes instead of seven. The **minor pentatonic** takes the natural minor scale and leaves out degrees 2 and 6:

**1 – b3 – 4 – 5 – b7**

In A: **A C D E G**.

("b3" means a minor third above the root, one half step below the major scale's 3rd. "b7" is likewise a minor 7th.)

Without the half steps of the full scale, no two notes clash. That makes the pentatonic scale forgiving for improvising: almost any note works over a matching chord.

steps.title: Position 1
steps.body:
The most used guitar fingering is a **box position** covering frets 5 to 8 for A minor pentatonic. Two notes per string:

| String | Frets | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | 5, 8 | A, C |
| 5 | 5, 7 | D, E |
| 4 | 5, 7 | G, A |
| 3 | 5, 7 | C, D |
| 2 | 5, 8 | E, G |
| 1 | 5, 8 | A, C |

Finger 1 plays every fret-5 note. Finger 3 plays fret 7, and finger 4 (or 3) plays fret 8. The root A is on strings 6 and 1 at fret 5, and on string 4 at fret 7.

steps.title: Position 1 up and down
steps.caption: From A on string 6 to C on string 1 and back.

exercise.prompt: A minor pentatonic, position 1, two octaves up and down. Alternate picking.

mistakeTips: Keep finger 1 anchored at fret 5 and let the other fingers reach.
Strings 6, 2, and 1 use frets 5 and 8; strings 5, 4, and 3 use frets 5 and 7.
The scale goes one note past two octaves, to C on string 1. Stop there and come back down.

questions.prompt: Which degrees make the minor pentatonic scale?
questions.explanation: Natural minor without 2 and 6.

questions.prompt: Spell E minor pentatonic.
questions.explanation: 1 E, b3 G, 4 A, 5 B, b7 D.

questions.prompt: In position 1 of A minor pentatonic, which fret does finger 1 cover?
questions.explanation: The box sits at frets 5 to 8.

questions.prompt: Why is the pentatonic scale forgiving to improvise with?
choices: It has no half steps that clash
questions.explanation: Removing degrees 2 and 6 removes the half steps.

params.scales: A minor pentatonic,E minor pentatonic,D minor pentatonic,G minor pentatonic

lessons.title: Bends, hammer-ons, pull-offs, and slides
lessons.summary: Learn the four techniques that make pentatonic lines sound like guitar, and check your bends against a target pitch.

steps.title: Hammer-ons and pull-offs
steps.body:
These let you play two notes with one pick stroke.

- **Hammer-on**: pick a note, then bring another finger down hard on a higher fret of the same string. The string keeps vibrating at the new pitch. Example: pick string 3 fret 5 (C), hammer finger 3 onto fret 7 (D).
- **Pull-off**: with two fingers down on one string, pick the higher note, then pull the higher finger off slightly sideways, plucking the string as you go. Example: fingers on string 2 frets 5 and 8, pick fret 8 (G), pull off to fret 5 (E).

Hammer with the fingertip, close to the fret. For a pull-off, the lower finger must already be pressing.

steps.title: Slides
steps.body:
A **slide** moves a finger along the string to a new fret while the note keeps sounding. Keep the same pressure while moving; lighten it and the note dies, press too hard and it squeaks.

Example: pick string 4 fret 5 (G) and slide finger 3 up to fret 7 (A). Slides connect the pentatonic positions too.

steps.title: Bends and vibrato
steps.body:
A **bend** pushes the string across the fretboard to raise its pitch. Most bends go up a **whole step** (2 frets' worth) or a **half step**.

- Use finger 3 for the bend, with fingers 1 and 2 behind it on the same string for support.
- Push from the wrist, turning it like opening a door, not by squeezing with the finger.
- Bend strings 1 to 3 toward the ceiling. The low strings are usually pulled toward the floor.

Target pitch matters. A whole-step bend on string 3 fret 7 (D) should reach **E**, the same pitch as string 2 fret 5. Out-of-tune bends are the most common lead-guitar problem.

**Vibrato** is a small, repeated bend-and-release that makes a held note sing.

The app hears pitch only, so it checks where a bend lands, not how you got there.

steps.title: The four techniques
steps.caption: Hammer-on C to D, pull-off G to E, slide G to A, then a bend from D up to E.

playback.rhythm: q q q q q q q q

exercise.prompt: Hammer-on and pull-off pairs: C to D (string 3, frets 5 to 7), then G to E (string 2, frets 8 to 5). Pick only the first note of each pair.

mistakeTips: If the hammered note is weak, snap the finger down faster, right behind the fret.
If the pull-off note is weak, pull the finger slightly toward the floor as it leaves the string.
Keep finger 1 pressing fret 5 throughout.

exercise.prompt: Bend string 3 at fret 7 up a whole step until it matches E (string 2, fret 5). Hold it there until the app accepts it. Play the target first if it helps.

mistakeTips: Support the bend with fingers 1 and 2 on frets 5 and 6.
Bend from the wrist. If the note stops short, push a little more.
If the app hears D# or a pitch between D# and E, you are bending only part of the way.

questions.prompt: How many times do you pick for a hammer-on from fret 5 to fret 7?
questions.explanation: Pick the first note; the hammer sounds the second.

questions.prompt: Which technique lowers the pitch without picking again?
questions.explanation: Pulling off a finger reveals the lower fretted note.

questions.prompt: A whole-step bend from D should reach…
questions.explanation: A whole step above D is E.

questions.prompt: Which part of the body should power a bend?
questions.explanation: Rotate the wrist like turning a door handle.

reviewItems.prompt: What is the difference between a hammer-on and a pull-off?
reviewItems.answer: Hammer-on: finger strikes a higher fret. Pull-off: finger leaves to reveal a lower fret. Both without picking again.

reviewItems.prompt: Whole-step bend from G reaches what note?

lessons.title: The five pentatonic positions
lessons.summary: Connect five box positions of A minor pentatonic to cover the whole neck.

steps.title: Five boxes, one scale
steps.body:
A minor pentatonic has only five notes, but they repeat all over the neck. Guitarists split the neck into **five positions**, each starting on the next note of the scale on string 6:

| Position | Starts on | Frets (about) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | A | 5–8 |
| 2 | C | 7–10 |
| 3 | D | 9–13 |
| 4 | E | 12–15 |
| 5 | G | 14–17 |

After position 5 the pattern repeats: position 1 again at fret 17, and also at fret 5 minus 12 (open position, frets 0 to 3).

Each position shares its lower notes with the position below and its upper notes with the one above. You connect them by sliding along a string.

steps.title: Position 2
steps.body:
Position 2 starts where position 1's upper notes are: C on string 6, fret 8.

Frets: string 6: 8, 10 · string 5: 7, 10 · string 4: 7, 10 · string 3: 7, 9 · string 2: 8, 10 · string 1: 8, 10.

Roots (A) are on string 4 fret 7 and string 2 fret 10.

steps.title: Position 3
steps.body:
Starts on D, string 6 fret 10.

Frets: string 6: 10, 12 · string 5: 10, 12 · string 4: 10, 12 · string 3: 9, 12 · string 2: 10, 13 · string 1: 10, 12.

steps.title: Position 4
steps.body:
Starts on E, string 6 fret 12.

Frets: string 6: 12, 15 · string 5: 12, 15 · string 4: 12, 14 · string 3: 12, 14 · string 2: 13, 15 · string 1: 12, 15.

steps.title: Position 5
steps.body:
Starts on G, string 6 fret 15.

Frets: string 6: 15, 17 · string 5: 15, 17 · string 4: 14, 17 · string 3: 14, 17 · string 2: 15, 17 · string 1: 15, 17.

On most acoustic guitars the upper frets are hard to reach past the body joint. Positions 1 to 3, plus the open position, are the most practical on acoustic.

exercise.prompt: Position 2 of A minor pentatonic, up from C on string 6, fret 8.

mistakeTips: Use one finger per fret: finger 1 on fret 7, 2 on 8, 3 on 9, 4 on 10.
String 3 uses frets 7 and 9; string 2 uses 8 and 10.
Say the note names as you go: C D E G A C D E G A C D.

exercise.prompt: Connect positions 1 and 2 on string 3: play C D E up the G string with slides (frets 5, 7, 9), then back down.

mistakeTips: Slide finger 3 from fret 7 to fret 9 to cross into position 2.
This is one of many ways to move between positions. Any string works.

questions.prompt: Which note starts position 2 of A minor pentatonic on string 6?
questions.explanation: The positions start on successive scale notes: A, C, D, E, G.

questions.prompt: After position 5, what comes next going up?
questions.explanation: The five positions repeat every 12 frets.

questions.prompt: How many different notes are in every position?
questions.explanation: Every position is the same five notes, A C D E G.

reviewItems.prompt: A minor pentatonic positions start on which notes on string 6?

lessons.title: Major pentatonic and the blues scale
lessons.summary: See the major pentatonic inside the minor one, and add the blue note to make the blues scale.

steps.title: Major pentatonic
steps.body:
The **major pentatonic scale** is the major scale without degrees 4 and 7: **1 – 2 – 3 – 5 – 6**. C major pentatonic is **C D E G A**.

Those are the same five notes as A minor pentatonic. Just as A minor is the relative minor of C major, **A minor pentatonic and C major pentatonic share notes**; only the home note changes. Every minor pentatonic position is also a major pentatonic position for the note three frets higher.

G major pentatonic in open position (G A B D E) is a friendly one for acoustic players, and it fits songs in G.

steps.title: The blues scale
steps.body:
Add one note to the minor pentatonic: the **b5**, a tritone above the root. The result is the **blues scale**: **1 – b3 – 4 – b5 – 5 – b7**.

In A: **A C D Eb E G**. In position 1 the Eb is at string 5 fret 6 and string 3 fret 8.

The b5 is a **blue note**: it sounds tense and is usually used as a passing note between 4 and 5, not held.

steps.title: Minor pentatonic, then blues scale
steps.caption: A minor pentatonic one octave, then the A blues scale one octave.

exercise.prompt: G major pentatonic, two octaves, open position.

mistakeTips: No note is on fret 1. Use fingers 2 and 3 for frets 2 and 3.
Start and end on G (string 6, fret 3) so the ear hears G as home.

exercise.prompt: A blues scale, position 1, from A on string 6 to A on string 1.

mistakeTips: The Eb on string 5 is fret 6: use finger 2.
On string 3, the Eb is fret 8: use finger 4.

questions.prompt: Which degrees make the major pentatonic?
questions.explanation: Major scale without 4 and 7.

questions.prompt: Which major pentatonic has the same notes as A minor pentatonic?
questions.explanation: Relative keys: A minor and C major.

questions.prompt: Which note does the blues scale add to the minor pentatonic?
questions.explanation: The flat 5th, e.g. Eb in A.

questions.prompt: Spell E blues scale.
choices: E G A Bb B D
E G A A# B D#
E F# G A B D
questions.explanation: E, b3 G, 4 A, b5 Bb, 5 B, b7 D.

lessons.title: Dominant 7ths and the 12-bar blues
lessons.summary: Play A7, D7, and E7, and learn the twelve-measure form behind countless blues and rock songs.

steps.title: Dominant seventh chords
steps.body:
Blues uses **dominant seventh chords**: a major triad plus a **minor seventh** above the root.

- **A7** = A C# E + **G**
- **D7** = D F# A + **C**
- **E7** = E G# B + **D**

The name "dominant" comes from its natural home on degree 5 (V7) of a major key. Blues uses it on I, IV, and V alike, which is part of its sound. Stage 8 covers seventh chords in full.

steps.title: Open 7th fingerings
steps.body:
- **A7**: finger 2 on string 4 fret 2, finger 3 on string 2 fret 2. Strum 5 to 1. (It is the A chord with string 3 left open, so that string rings as G.)
- **D7**: finger 2 on string 3 fret 2, finger 1 on string 2 fret 1, finger 3 on string 1 fret 2. Strum 4 to 1.
- **E7**: finger 2 on string 5 fret 2, finger 1 on string 3 fret 1. Strum all six. (E with finger 3 lifted, so string 4 rings open as D.)

steps.title: The 12-bar form
steps.body:
The **twelve-bar blues** is a 12-measure cycle of I, IV, and V:

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | I | I | I |
| IV | IV | I | I |
| V | IV | I | V |

In A: **A7 A7 A7 A7 | D7 D7 A7 A7 | E7 D7 A7 E7**.

- Measure 12 on V is the **turnaround**: it sets up the return to measure 1.
- A common variant, the **quick change**, goes to IV in measure 2 and back to I in measure 3.
- Lyrics often follow the same plan: a line, the line repeated, and an answering line, one per four measures.

steps.title: 12 bars in A
steps.caption: One chord strum per beat, one time through.

playback.rhythm: q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q

mistakeTips: A7: string 3 must ring open. Arch finger 2.
D7: skip strings 6 and 5.
E7: string 4 rings open. Keep finger 2 off it.

exercise.prompt: 12-bar blues in A: four downstrokes per measure. Follow the chord shown.

mistakeTips: Count measures as well as beats: "1 2 3 4, 2 2 3 4, 3 2 3 4…".
The change to D7 comes after four measures of A7. The E7 comes in measure 9.
Measure 12 is E7, not A7. It leads back to the top.

questions.prompt: Spell A7.
questions.explanation: Major triad + minor 7th (G).

questions.prompt: What chord is in measure 5 of a 12-bar blues in A?
questions.explanation: Measures 5–6 are IV.

questions.prompt: What is the V chord of a 12-bar blues in E?
questions.explanation: E F# G# A B: V = B, so B7.

questions.prompt: What is a quick change?
questions.explanation: I – IV – I – I in the first four measures.

questions.prompt: What is the turnaround's job?
questions.explanation: V in the last measure pulls back to I.

reviewItems.answer: I I I I | IV IV I I | V IV I V
Major triad plus a minor 7th: 1 3 5 b7.

lessons.title: First improvisation
lessons.summary: Make up your own phrases over a 12-bar blues using call and response and a few simple rules.

steps.title: Improvising is choosing
steps.body:
**Improvisation** means making up music on the spot. It is less mysterious than it sounds: you choose from a small set of notes (A minor pentatonic) and a small set of rhythms, and you group them into **phrases**.

Start with rules that limit your choices:

1. Use only three notes at first: A, C, and D in position 1 (string 4 fret 7, string 3 frets 5 and 7).
2. Play short phrases of 2 to 4 beats, then **rest** as long as you played.
3. End phrases on **A**, the root. It always sounds finished.
4. Repeat a phrase you like. Repetition sounds intentional.

steps.title: Call and response
steps.body:
**Call and response** is a musical conversation: a phrase (the call), then an answer (the response). Blues is built on it.

A simple way in: play a phrase, then answer it with the same rhythm but a different last note. Or copy the app's phrase exactly, then change one thing.

steps.title: A call
steps.caption: A two-measure phrase in A minor pentatonic, ending on A.

playback.rhythm: q q h q q h

exercise.prompt: Echo the call: play it back exactly.

mistakeTips: It starts on C (string 3, fret 5) and ends on A (string 4, fret 7).
Sing it first. If you can sing it, you can find it.

exercise.prompt: Improvise over the 12-bar blues in A for one minute using A minor pentatonic. Follow the rules: short phrases, rests, end on A.

mistakeTips: Leave space. Rests are part of the phrase.
Fewer notes, played with good timing, sound better than many rushed notes.
Try a bend from D to E (string 3, fret 7) to end a phrase with some tension.
The grade counts notes in the scale and steady rhythm. It does not judge taste.

questions.prompt: Which note is the safest place to end a phrase over A blues?
questions.explanation: The root sounds settled.

questions.prompt: What is call and response?
choices: A phrase answered by another phrase
questions.explanation: A musical question and answer.

questions.prompt: Why leave rests between phrases?
choices: They separate ideas and let the music breathe
questions.explanation: Rests separate ideas the way pauses separate sentences.

reviewItems.prompt: Name three simple rules for a first improvisation.
reviewItems.answer: Few notes; short phrases with rests; end on the root.

lessons.title: Blues review: a 12-bar head
lessons.summary: Review pentatonic scales, techniques, and the 12-bar form, then play a 12-bar rhythm part and an original melody over it.

steps.title: What you know now
steps.body:
- Minor pentatonic **1 b3 4 5 b7**, major pentatonic **1 2 3 5 6**, blues scale **1 b3 4 b5 5 b7**.
- Five positions cover the neck.
- Hammer-ons, pull-offs, slides, and bends; bends must reach a target pitch.
- 12-bar blues: **I I I I | IV IV I I | V IV I V** with dominant 7th chords.
- Improvise with short phrases, rests, and strong endings.

questions.prompt: Spell D minor pentatonic.
choices: D F G Ab A C
questions.explanation: 1 D, b3 F, 4 G, 5 A, b7 C.

questions.prompt: Which scale adds the b5 to the minor pentatonic?
In a 12-bar blues in G, which chord is in measure 9?
questions.explanation: Measure 9 is V: D7.

questions.prompt: Which technique raises pitch by pushing the string sideways?
questions.explanation: A bend changes pitch without changing fret.

steps.title: A 12-bar head
steps.body:
A **head** is the main melody of a blues or jazz tune. This one is original and uses only A minor pentatonic in position 1: A (4 fret 7), C (3 fret 5), D (3 fret 7), E (2 fret 5), G (2 fret 8), high A (1 fret 5), and low E (5 fret 7).

Notice the call-and-response plan: measures 1–4 are a call, 5–8 answer it over D7, and 9–12 close the form.

branches.title: Blues shuffle
branches.summary: The shuffle feel, power chords, and the boogie rhythm through a full 12-bar blues. Optional.

lessons.title: The shuffle feel
lessons.summary: Turn straight eighth notes into a long-short triplet shuffle.

steps.title: Long-short
steps.body:
A **shuffle** plays each beat as a long note and a short note. It comes from the triplet: divide the beat into three, hold through the first two parts, and play again on the third.

Count: "**1** – a **2** – a **3** – a **4** – a". Many players hear it as "**doo**-ba **doo**-ba".

Keep the picking hand moving in steady triplets: down (play), up (miss), down (play)... or simply down-up with the upstroke late. Either way, the feel is uneven on purpose.

diagram.rhythm: tq te tq te tq te tq te
diagram.caption: Shuffle eighths: long-short on every beat.

steps.title: Straight, then shuffled
steps.caption: Open A string: one measure of straight eighths, then one of shuffle.

playback.rhythm: e e e e e e e e tq te tq te tq te tq te

exercise.prompt: Open A string: two measures of shuffle eighths.
exercise.rhythm: tq te tq te tq te tq te tq te tq te tq te tq te

mistakeTips: Say "doo-ba doo-ba" out loud while you play.
The short note sits just before the next beat, not halfway.
If it sounds straight, make the first note longer.

reviewItems.prompt: How is a shuffle beat divided?
reviewItems.answer: Into a triplet: long note on the first two parts, short note on the third.

lessons.title: Power chords and the boogie pattern
lessons.summary: Play A5, D5, and E5, and add the sixth to make the classic boogie rhythm.

steps.title: Power chords
steps.body:
A **power chord** has only a root and a perfect fifth, written with a 5: **A5** = A + E. With no third it is neither major nor minor, so it fits under blues melodies that mix major and minor sounds.

Open power chords, two strings each:

- **A5**: open string 5 + string 4 fret 2.
- **D5**: open string 4 + string 3 fret 2.
- **E5**: open string 6 + string 5 fret 2.

steps.title: Adding the sixth
steps.body:
The **boogie pattern** alternates the power chord with a **dyad** (two notes) of the root and the 6th: stretch finger 3 two frets past finger 1.

For A: A+E (fret 2), A+E, A+F# (fret 4), A+F#, repeating. The same move works for D on strings 4 and 3, and for E on strings 6 and 5.

Played with a shuffle feel, this is the rhythm part of a great many blues and early rock songs.

playback.rhythm: tq te tq te tq te tq te tq te tq te tq te tq te

exercise.prompt: Strum A5, D5, then E5 in shuffle eighths, one measure each. Hit only the two strings of each chord.
exercise.rhythm: tq te tq te tq te tq te

mistakeTips: Aim the pick at the root string and stop after the next string.
Rest the side of your picking hand on the bridge-end of the strings for a tighter, muted sound.
Keep finger 1 down; only finger 3 moves for the sixth.

steps.title: Boogie in A, two measures
steps.caption: Fret 2, fret 2, fret 4, fret 4, twice per measure.
steps.rhythm: tq te tq te tq te tq te tq te tq te tq te tq te

lessons.title: 12-bar shuffle in A
lessons.summary: Put the boogie pattern through the full 12-bar blues form.

steps.title: Moving the pattern
steps.body:
Use the boogie pattern on each chord of the 12-bar form:

- A measures: strings 5 and 4 (A with E, F#).
- D measures: strings 4 and 3 (D with A, B).
- E measures: strings 6 and 5 (E with B, C#).

Form: **A A A A | D D A A | E D A E**.

exercise.prompt: Warm-up: A5, D5, E5 changes for one minute.

mistakeTips: The finger pattern is the same on each string pair; only the strings change.
Look ahead to the next string pair at the end of each measure.
